content:
Christian preachers often put it to Muslims in a single line: the Bible calls Jesus (peace be upon him) the Son of God, and a son of God shares the nature of God, so the Bible teaches that he is God.[1]

The title is real, and the New Testament gives it to Jesus with weight. The Bible also gives it to angels, to a nation, to kings, to peacemakers, to believers and to Adam. What the title means has to be read from each passage.

This article aims to provide context to that argument, insha'Allah, in seven uses of "son of God" in the Bible, each read in its setting. The Quran states its own rule at the outset: "He begetteth not, nor is He begotten; And there is none like unto Him" (112:3 to 4).[2]

"Now on the day when God's sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them" (Job 1:6). At creation, "the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy" (Job 38:7).[3]

The Hebrew is benē hāʾĕlōhîm. The phrase names members of the heavenly court, creatures who stand before God and answer to Him. Nobody reads Job as saying that God fathered them.

"God's sons saw that men's daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives" (Genesis 6:2).[3] Who they were has been argued since antiquity.

1 Enoch read them as fallen angels; many Christian interpreters read them as the descendants of Seth; others as rulers. John Day sets the passage beside older Canaanite traditions of divine beings, and J. J. T. Doedens has surveyed the whole history of its interpretation.[4] On every reading, the sons of Genesis 6 are creatures.

"You shall tell Pharaoh, 'Yahweh says, Israel is my son, my firstborn'" (Exodus 4:22). Hosea recalls it: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt" (Hosea 11:1).[3]

Here the son is a whole people. The word speaks of election, covenant and care, and no Jewish reader has taken it to mean that Israel shares God's nature. Matthew later applies Hosea 11:1 to Jesus (Matthew 2:15), the same words used of the nation.[3]

God promises David concerning his heir: "I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men" (2 Samuel 7:14). At the king's coronation: "You are my son. Today I have become your father" (Psalm 2:7).[3]

A son who may commit iniquity and be chastened is a man. Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm, and "today" marks the day of enthronement. The New Testament later reads the psalm of Jesus; in its first setting, it speaks of a king of Judah.

Jesus said: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God" (Matthew 5:9). Paul wrote: "as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God", and spoke of receiving "the Spirit of adoption" (Romans 8:14 to 15).[3]

Kyu Seop Kim reads Paul's adoption against Roman legal practice: the believer is made a son by a legal act of favour.[5] Sonship here is a status given to creatures, by conduct or by adoption.

Luke's genealogy of Jesus ends: "the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God" (Luke 3:38).[3]

Adam had no human father, and Luke calls him son of God for that reason. The Quran draws the same comparison and reaches the opposite conclusion from the Christian one: "The similitude of Jesus before Allah is as that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: 'Be'. And he was" (3:59).[2]

The New Testament gives Jesus the title in a special way. Mark sets it at his baptism and at the cross, where the centurion says, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39), and John calls believers "God's children" while keeping the singular title for Jesus (John 1:12).[3]

When he was accused of blasphemy for it, John records his defence. "Isn't it written in your law, 'I said, you are gods?' If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came... do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, 'You blaspheme,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God?'" (John 10:34 to 36), quoting Psalm 82:6: "You are gods, all of you are sons of the Most High."[6]

Jesus answered the charge by setting his title beside the "gods" of Psalm 82, those "to whom the word of God came", and by describing himself as one "sanctified and sent". Michael Peppard has argued that divine sonship in the first century has to be read in its Jewish and Roman settings before the creeds of the fourth are read into it.[7] The Gospel's own account of the title begins with a man sent by God.

The bottom line

The Bible calls angels, Israel, the kings of David's line, peacemakers, believers and Adam sons of God, and none of them is God for it. The New Testament gives Jesus the title in a singular way, and his own defence of it, in John 10, sets it beside the "gods" of Psalm 82 and calls him the one God "sent into the world".

The Quran answers the claim of sonship for every people alike. When Jews and Christians said "We are sons of Allah, and his beloved", it replied: "Nay, ye are but men,- of the men he hath created" (5:18).[2] "It is not consonant with the majesty of (Allah) Most Gracious that He should beget a son" (19:92). We set out the wider case in 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The argument is common in Christian preaching to Muslims. The Bismikaa archive answered it in Ketuhanan Yesus dan Tanggapannya and Pertentangan sifat Yesus sebagai TUHAN ALLAH di dalam Perjanjian Baru.
  2. Quran 112:3 to 4; 3:59; 5:18; 19:88 to 92, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Job 1:6; 38:7; Genesis 6:1 to 4; Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:15; 2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7; Matthew 5:9; Romans 8:14 to 17; Luke 3:23 to 38; Mark 1:11; 15:39; John 1:12 (World English Bible).
  4. John Day, "The Sons of God and Daughters of Men and the Giants: Disputed Points in the Interpretation of Genesis 6:1–4", Hebrew Bible and Ancient Israel 1, no. 4 (2012), pp. 427–447; J. J. T. Doedens, The Sons of God in Genesis 6:1–4: Analysis and History of Exegesis (Leiden: Brill, 2019).
  5. Kyu Seop Kim, "Another Look at Adoption in Romans 8:15 in Light of Roman Social Practices and Legal Rules", Biblical Theology Bulletin 44, no. 3 (2014), pp. 133–143.
  6. John 10:31 to 36; Psalm 82:1 to 8 (World English Bible).
  7. Michael Peppard, The Son of God in the Roman World: Divine Sonship in Its Social and Political Context (New York: Oxford University Press, 2011).
